title: Walking in Truth
overview: 3 John is a personal letter from the Apostle John addressing Gaius, a beloved brother in the faith. The chapter emphasizes the importance of walking in truth, showing hospitality to traveling missionaries, and resisting divisive behavior within the church. John commends Gaius for his faithfulness and love, contrasts this with the arrogance and rejection of Diotrephes, and encourages believers to imitate what is good. The letter highlights the practical outworking of Christian love and truth in community life, underscoring the need to support those who labor for the gospel and to reject evil influences. This brief epistle offers timeless guidance on church unity, hospitality, and godly conduct.
structure:
**Verses 1-4: Greeting and Commendation.** John opens by expressing his love for Gaius in the truth and rejoices over the testimony of Gaius’s faithful walk in the truth, emphasizing the joy of spiritual children living rightly.

**Verses 5-8: Praise for Hospitality.** John commends Gaius for his faithful service to both brethren and strangers, particularly for supporting traveling missionaries who preach the gospel without seeking material gain, urging the church to receive such workers.

**Verses 9-10: Reproof of Diotrephes.** John addresses the disruptive behavior of Diotrephes, who refuses to welcome John’s messengers, speaks maliciously against them, and exerts authoritarian control by excluding others from the church.

**Verses 11-12: Exhortation and Commendation.** John advises Gaius to imitate what is good and avoid evil, affirming that those who do good are of God. He also commends Demetrius, who has a good reputation and is a faithful witness to the truth.

**Verses 13-14: Closing Remarks.** John concludes with a personal note, expressing his desire to visit Gaius soon and sending greetings from mutual friends, emphasizing fellowship and peace.

keyVerses.text: I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the deep spiritual joy that comes from seeing believers live faithfully in the truth of the gospel, underscoring the importance of genuine Christian discipleship and obedience.

keyVerses.text: Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers;
keyVerses.significance: John commends Gaius’s faithful hospitality and service, emphasizing the biblical mandate to care for both fellow believers and strangers, reflecting Christ’s love in practical ways.

keyVerses.text: We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth.
keyVerses.significance: This verse stresses the responsibility of the church to support gospel workers, recognizing that hospitality is a partnership in advancing the truth of Christ.

keyVerses.text: Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good. He that doeth good is of God: but he that doeth evil hath not seen God.
keyVerses.significance: John’s exhortation here draws a clear moral line between good and evil, linking ethical behavior directly to one’s relationship with God, a central theme in Christian living.

keyVerses.text: I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
keyVerses.significance: This verse introduces the conflict with Diotrephes, illustrating the dangers of pride and divisiveness within the church, and the importance of humility and submission to apostolic authority.

characters.name: John the Elder
characters.description: The author of the epistle, a respected church leader who writes to encourage faithfulness, hospitality, and truth, while addressing issues of church discipline and unity.

characters.name: Gaius
characters.description: The recipient of the letter, commended for his faithful walk in truth and generous hospitality toward traveling missionaries, serving as a model believer.

characters.name: Diotrephes
characters.description: A church leader who rejects John’s authority, refuses to welcome the apostolic messengers, and exerts divisive control, embodying pride and opposition to the gospel’s unity.

characters.name: Demetrius
characters.description: A well-regarded believer commended for his good testimony and faithfulness to the truth, representing the positive example of Christian character.

themes.description: The chapter emphasizes living consistently in the truth of the gospel, reflecting authentic faith and obedience, which is foundational to Christian identity and witness.

themes.theme: Hospitality and Support for Gospel Workers
themes.description: Gaius’s hospitality to traveling missionaries highlights the biblical call to support those who labor for the gospel, reinforcing the partnership between believers and ministers.

The conflict with Diotrephes illustrates the challenges of maintaining order and humility within the church, underscoring the need for submission to godly leadership and correction of divisive behavior.
John contrasts good and evil actions as markers of one’s relationship with God, encouraging believers to imitate what is good and reject evil influences.

historicalContext: 3 John was written in the late first century AD, likely from Ephesus or another city in Asia Minor, to address issues within early Christian house churches. During this period, Christianity was still a minority faith within the Roman Empire, often meeting in private homes. Hospitality was a critical cultural value, especially for traveling teachers and missionaries who depended on the support of local believers. The church was also grappling with internal conflicts over authority and doctrinal purity, as false teachings and prideful leaders threatened unity. The letter reflects these dynamics, encouraging faithful conduct and proper reception of apostolic messengers in a context where church structure was informal but vital for the spread of the gospel.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology highlights the sovereignty of God in preserving the truth and the importance of church discipline as seen in the rebuke of Diotrephes. The emphasis on walking in truth aligns with sanctification as evidence of genuine faith.

Dispensationalists focus on the practical instructions for church order and hospitality, viewing the letter as a timeless guide for local church governance and support of missionary work within the present church age.
Early church fathers saw this epistle as emphasizing love and truth as inseparable in Christian life, with hospitality being a tangible expression of faith and a safeguard against heresy and schism.

crossReferences.connection: Encourages hospitality to strangers, paralleling Gaius’s faithful service to traveling brethren.
Reminds believers to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing so some have entertained angels unaware, echoing the chapter’s emphasis on receiving gospel workers.
Outlines qualifications for church leaders, relevant to the issues of authority and behavior seen in Diotrephes’s conduct.
Jesus as the way, truth, and life connects to the theme of walking in truth in this epistle.
Calls believers to do good to all, especially to those of the household of faith, reinforcing the chapter’s call to faithful service.

application: Cultivate a consistent walk in the truth by grounding your life daily in Scripture and obedience to God’s commands.
Practice hospitality by supporting missionaries and church workers, recognizing this as a partnership in the gospel.
Reject prideful and divisive attitudes within the church, submitting instead to godly leadership and promoting unity.
Discern between good and evil actions as evidence of one’s relationship with God, striving to imitate what is good.
Encourage and affirm faithful believers in their service to strengthen the body of Christ.
Seek personal fellowship and accountability with fellow believers to maintain spiritual health and peace.
conclusion: 3 John offers believers a timeless exhortation to live faithfully in the truth, demonstrating love through hospitality and support for gospel workers. It warns against pride and division, urging submission to godly authority and imitation of good. The chapter’s focus on practical Christian living within the community challenges believers today to embody truth in their relationships and church life, fostering unity and advancing the gospel with joy and integrity.
timeline: c. AD 85-95 - Late First Century Apostolic Era

definitions.definition: A church leader or overseer responsible for teaching, pastoral care, and governance within the early Christian community.
In the KJV context, refers to Christian love expressed through generous and selfless actions toward others.
The state of being first in rank or authority, often associated with prideful ambition in a leadership context.
Those who assist or partner with others in a shared mission, particularly in advancing the truth of the gospel.

outline.heading: Greeting and Commendation
outline.description: John opens with a warm greeting to Gaius, expressing love and joy over his faithful walk in the truth, setting a tone of encouragement and spiritual affirmation.

outline.heading: Praise for Hospitality
outline.description: John commends Gaius for his generous support of traveling missionaries, emphasizing the importance of hospitality as a means of partnering in the gospel.

outline.heading: Reproof of Diotrephes
outline.description: John addresses the problematic behavior of Diotrephes, who rejects apostolic authority and disrupts church unity through pride and exclusion.

outline.heading: Exhortation and Commendation
outline.description: John urges Gaius to imitate good and avoid evil, affirming Demetrius as a positive example of faithfulness and good testimony.

outline.heading: Closing Remarks
outline.description: John concludes with a personal note of anticipated fellowship and greetings, emphasizing peace and mutual encouragement among believers.
